items.text: An agent is an LLM in a loop: it observes the current state, decides on an action, calls a tool, reads the result, and repeats until the goal is met or a limit is hit.
The environment is the agent's ground truth. Each tool result tells the agent whether its last step worked, so it can correct course instead of guessing.
Every agent loop needs explicit stop conditions: task complete, max steps, max cost, or an unrecoverable error. Without them a confused agent can run forever.
Workflows run LLM calls along predefined code paths; agents let the model choose the path. Use an agent only when the steps cannot be known in advance.
The model never runs a tool itself. It emits a structured tool call, your code executes it, and you send the result back as the next message.
Errors compound over steps: if each step succeeds 95% of the time, a 20-step task succeeds only about 36% of the time. Cut steps or add checks between them.
Give the agent a clear definition of done. 'Improve the code' invites endless wandering; 'make these three tests pass' has a finish line.
Start simple: a single well-prompted LLM call with good retrieval often beats an agent. Add loops and autonomy only when evals show you need them.
Good agent tasks are open-ended, multi-step and verifiable, with room for trial and error. Poor fits need one right answer on the first try with no feedback.
Be wary of frameworks that hide prompts and tool calls. Start with direct API calls so you know exactly what the model sees, then abstract if needed.
Ask how cheap a mistake is to detect and undo. Agents shine where errors are recoverable and need heavy guardrails where one wrong action is costly.
Name tools like functions for a new teammate: search_customer_orders beats query or tool2. The model picks tools largely from names and descriptions.
Write tool descriptions like docs for a new hire: what the tool does, when to use it, when not to, and what each parameter means, ideally with an example.
Use typed schemas with enums, required fields and formats. 'status: one of open, closed' stops the model from inventing values like 'done'.
Good tool errors teach recovery: 'date must be YYYY-MM-DD, got 03/04' beats a bare 'invalid input' or a raw stack trace.
Fewer, well-scoped tools beat many overlapping ones. If two tools could plausibly handle the same request, the model will choose between them inconsistently.
Design tools around tasks, not raw endpoints. One schedule_meeting tool beats making the agent chain list_users, check_calendar and create_event itself.
Return only what the agent needs. Paginate, truncate or summarize large tool responses, and offer a detailed mode the agent can request when necessary.
Return human-meaningful fields like names and titles instead of opaque UUIDs where possible. Models reason more reliably over semantic identifiers.
Namespace related tools with a shared prefix, like github_create_issue and github_list_prs, so the agent can tell which system each tool touches.
Avoid parameters that demand fiddly formatting, like code escaped inside JSON strings. Choose input formats the model naturally writes correctly.
Test tools by watching the agent use them. Repeated wrong parameters or misused calls point to unclear names or descriptions you can fix.
Parallel tool calls let the model request several independent lookups in one turn, saving round trips. Make sure those tools are safe to run concurrently.
ReAct interleaves reasoning and acting: the model writes a thought, takes an action, reads the observation, and reasons again, grounding its plan in real results.
ReAct beats pure reasoning on knowledge tasks because it can look facts up, and beats pure acting because explicit thoughts keep it on track.
Reactive agents pick one step at a time from the latest observation. Simple and adaptive, but they can lose sight of the overall goal on long tasks.
Plan-and-execute agents draft a full plan first, then work through it. Plans make progress visible and reviewable, but must be revised when reality differs.
Keep the plan in a visible, updatable artifact such as a todo list. Updating it after each step keeps the agent oriented and lets humans follow along.
Replan on surprise: when a tool result contradicts an assumption, the agent should revise the plan rather than push ahead with stale steps.
Reflection: after an attempt, the agent critiques its output against the goal and revises. It works best when the critique uses concrete signals like test results.
Self-critique without external feedback has limits: a model often misses its own errors and may 'fix' correct answers. Ground critique in real checks.
Record lessons from failed attempts, such as 'this API needs header X', so the next try starts smarter instead of repeating the same mistake.
Ask for a specific critique: requirements not met, edge cases missed, claims lacking evidence. A vague 'is this good?' gets a reflexive yes.
Short-term memory is the context window: the running conversation and tool results. It is precise but finite, and it vanishes when the session ends.
Long-term memory lives outside the model, in files, databases or vector stores, and is retrieved into the context only when it is relevant.
Summarization memory compresses older turns into a running summary, keeping decisions, open questions and key findings while dropping verbose tool output.
Let the agent write progress notes and decisions to a file, so work survives context resets and a fresh session can pick up where the last one stopped.
Memory needs curation: stale or wrong memories get retrieved and reinforced. Timestamp entries and let newer facts supersede older ones.
Memory is an attack surface: one poisoned entry can steer every future session. Treat recalled memories as untrusted input, not as instructions.
Context engineering is deciding what enters the window at each step: instructions, tools, history, retrieved data. The agent can only act on what it sees.
Load context just in time: give the agent lightweight references like file paths or IDs plus tools to fetch details, instead of preloading everything.
Clear old tool results once they have been used. A raw 5,000-line log from ten steps ago rarely helps and crowds out what matters now.
Set a context budget per component: system prompt, tool definitions, history and retrieved data. Watch which part grows as tasks get longer.
Tool definitions cost tokens on every call. Dozens of rarely used tools waste budget and muddle selection, so load tools on demand when you can.
Recency matters: in a long agent context, put the most decision-relevant facts and the current objective last, right before the model chooses its next action.
Sub-agents isolate context: a worker can burn many tokens exploring, then return a short summary, keeping the main agent's window clean.
Prompt chaining: break a task into fixed sequential LLM calls, each consuming the previous output. Add programmatic checks between steps to catch errors early.
Routing: classify the input first, then send it to a specialized prompt, tool set or model. Separating cases keeps each handler simple and well tuned.
Parallelization by sectioning splits a task into independent parts that run at once, such as one call answering while another screens for policy issues.
Parallelization by voting runs the same task several times and aggregates the verdicts, useful for high-stakes judgments like flagging vulnerable code.
Orchestrator-worker: a lead agent breaks the task into subtasks at runtime, delegates them to workers, and synthesizes their results into one answer.
Evaluator-optimizer: one call generates, another evaluates against clear criteria and gives feedback, and the loop repeats until the output passes.
Multi-agent systems use many times more tokens than a single agent. They pay off for broad, parallelizable work, not for tightly coupled tasks.
Give each sub-agent a complete brief: objective, output format, tools and boundaries. Workers do not share the lead's context and will duplicate or miss work.
Tightly interdependent work, like many edits to one codebase, often goes worse with several agents: conflicting changes outweigh the parallel speed.
Scale effort to the query: a simple lookup needs one agent and a few calls, while a broad research question may justify several parallel workers.
MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard for connecting AI applications to tools and data, so one integration can work across many clients.
MCP roles: the host is the AI application, it creates one client per connection, and each server is a program that exposes capabilities to it.
MCP servers expose three main primitives: tools (actions the model can call), resources (data the app can read) and prompts (reusable templates).
In MCP, tools are model-controlled, resources are application-controlled and prompts are user-controlled. That split decides who triggers each one.
MCP servers run locally over stdio or remotely over HTTP. Remote servers typically use OAuth, so users grant scoped access instead of pasting keys.
An MCP server's tool descriptions flow straight into the model's context, so a malicious or compromised server can use them to inject instructions.
Install only MCP servers you trust, pin their versions and review what they can access. A server can change its tool definitions after you approve it.
MCP clients discover capabilities at runtime by listing a server's tools, so connecting a new server extends an agent without changing its code.
Human-in-the-loop: pause for approval before irreversible or high-impact actions like sending email, spending money, deleting data or deploying.
Make approvals meaningful by showing exactly what will happen: the diff, the recipient, the amount. Vague prompts train people to click approve blindly.
Tier permissions by risk: auto-allow reads, confirm writes, and require explicit sign-off for destructive or externally visible actions.
Let agents ask a clarifying question when a request is ambiguous. One question up front is cheaper than a long run in the wrong direction.
Checkpoint long tasks at milestones, such as after the plan or the first draft, so a human can redirect early instead of reviewing a finished mess.
Give agents least privilege: scoped credentials, read-only access by default, and only the tools the current task actually needs.
Run code-executing agents in a sandbox, such as a container or VM with no production credentials, restricted network access and a disposable filesystem.
Enforce guardrails in code, not only in the prompt. 'Never delete files' in a system prompt is a request; a permission check is a guarantee.
Input guardrails screen requests before the agent acts; output guardrails check actions and responses before they take effect. Use both.
Cap agent actions per run: max emails sent, max spend, max files changed. Hard caps turn a runaway bug into a small incident.
Lethal trifecta: an agent with private data, exposure to untrusted content and a way to send data out can be tricked into leaking. Remove one of the three.
Any tool that returns outside content, like web pages, emails, tickets or files, can carry prompt injection. Tool output is data, never instructions.
An instruction hidden in a fetched web page can make a browsing agent act for the attacker, using your credentials and your tools.
Wrap untrusted tool output in clearly labeled tags marking it as external content, and tell the model never to follow instructions found inside.
Labeling untrusted content helps but guarantees nothing. The real defense is limiting what the agent can do after it has read untrusted input.
Quarantine pattern: a privileged model plans using trusted input only, while a separate model with no tool access processes untrusted content.
Make agent actions idempotent: calling a tool twice with the same input should not create two orders or send two emails. Agents retry more than you expect.
Pass an idempotency key with write operations, so a tool call retried after a timeout is recognized and not executed a second time.
Prefer reversible actions: drafts over sends, soft deletes over hard deletes, feature branches over pushes to the main branch.
Have agents work on a copy, such as a branch, a staging environment or a dry-run mode, and apply changes for real only after review.
Snapshot state before risky steps, with a git commit or a database backup, so a bad agent action is one rollback away from undone.
Trace every agent run: each model call, prompt, tool call, arguments, result, latency and token count. You cannot debug what you cannot replay.
Structure traces as nested spans (run, step, model call, tool call) so you can see where time and tokens go and exactly where a run went wrong.
Monitor metrics across runs: success rate, steps per task, cost per task and tool error rates. Shifts in these flag regressions early.
Review failed trajectories regularly. The same tool misused or the same dead end repeated points to a specific prompt or tool fix.
Tag every trace with the prompt, model and tool versions used, so you can compare runs before and after a change.
Evaluate agents on task success first: did the final state meet the goal? Check the outcome in the environment, not the agent's own claim of success.
Trajectory evals examine the path: right tools, sensible order, no wasted or dangerous steps. Two successful runs can differ widely in cost and risk.
Do not grade agents against one 'correct' path. Agents often find valid alternatives, so grade outcomes and flag only clearly bad steps.
Run each agent eval task several times. Report the pass rate and, for reliability-critical uses, how often all k attempts succeed.
Build agent evals in realistic, resettable environments, like a test repo or sandboxed account, so every run starts from the same state.
When an agent hits its budget, have it return partial results with a clear status of what is done and what remains, instead of failing silently.
Avoid rereading the same large file or rerunning the same search every step. Cache tool results within a run while their inputs are unchanged.
Loop failure: the agent repeats the same action expecting a new result. Detect repeated identical tool calls and force a change of strategy or a stop.
Goal drift: over long runs an agent can quietly swap the user's goal for an easier nearby one. Restate the objective and check work against it.
Overconfidence: agents often declare success without verifying. Require evidence, like a passing test or a fetched confirmation, before 'done'.
Error cascades: one wrong early assumption, like a misread file path, poisons every later step. Verify key assumptions before building on them.
Tool hallucination: agents sometimes call tools or parameters that do not exist. Validate calls against the schema and reply with the valid options.
Coding agents may game tests: special-casing test inputs or weakening assertions to turn them green. Review any changes to tests closely.
Tests are a coding agent's best feedback signal. Write or find a failing test first, then let the agent iterate until it passes.
Keep diffs small and focused. Small changes are easier for the agent to get right and for humans to review; big rewrites hide bugs.
Have a coding agent explore and plan before editing: read the relevant files, propose an approach, then implement. It prevents confident edits in the wrong place.
Document project conventions in a file the agent reads at startup: build and test commands, code style, and things to avoid.
Commit working checkpoints often during coding sessions, so each commit marks a known-good state the agent can diff against when something breaks.
Review agent-written code like a colleague's pull request. Watch for unrequested changes, deleted tests and plausible APIs that do not exist.
When an agent keeps failing, reset instead of piling on corrections. A fresh session with a sharper prompt often beats a long, confused one.
